objectives: Distinguish kinematics from kinetics and apply Newton's laws to human movement.
Explain ground-reaction force, force plates, torque, and the three classes of lever in the body.
Describe how center of mass, gait analysis, and motion capture are used in a biomechanics laboratory.

slides.title: Kinematics, kinetics, and Newton's laws of movement
slides.body:
**Biomechanics** applies the principles of mechanics to living organisms. In sport it explains how athletes move, how forces are produced and absorbed, and how technique can be made safer and faster. The field divides naturally into two complementary halves.

**Kinematics** is the description of motion without reference to its causes. It deals with **position**, **displacement**, **velocity**, and **acceleration**, and with their angular counterparts **angular displacement**, **angular velocity**, and **angular acceleration**. A coach who films a sprinter and measures stride length, stride frequency, and joint angles is doing kinematics. Crucially, kinematics answers what is happening but not why.

**Kinetics**, by contrast, is the study of the **forces** that cause motion. It deals with **force**, **torque**, **momentum**, **impulse**, **work**, and **power**. A scientist who measures the force a sprinter applies to the track is doing kinetics. The distinction is fundamental: two athletes can have identical kinematics (the same visible movement) yet very different kinetics (different internal forces and joint loads), which matters greatly for performance and injury.

Both halves rest on **Isaac Newton's** three laws of motion, published in the **Principia** in **1687**:

- **First law (inertia)**: a body remains at rest or in uniform motion unless acted on by a net external force. An athlete coasting on ice keeps gliding until friction or another force intervenes.
- **Second law**: the net force equals mass times acceleration, $F = ma$, or more generally force equals the rate of change of **momentum**, $F = \frac{dp}{dt}$. This is the workhorse equation of kinetics; it links the force a runner applies to the acceleration of their body.
- **Third law**: for every action there is an equal and opposite reaction. When a runner pushes back and down on the ground, the ground pushes forward and up on the runner with an equal force, the **ground-reaction force**.

To these, angular analysis adds **Newton-Euler** rotational equations, in which **torque** equals the rate of change of **angular momentum**. Many athletic skills, from a diver's somersault to a discus throw, are best understood as the **conservation of angular momentum**: with no external torque, pulling the limbs inward reduces the moment of inertia and speeds the spin, exactly as a figure skater does. Newtonian mechanics, three and a half centuries old, remains the bedrock of every biomechanical analysis.

slides.title: Ground-reaction force, force plates, and torque
slides.body:
When an athlete contacts the ground, **Newton's third law** guarantees an equal and opposite **ground-reaction force (GRF)**. The GRF is a vector with three components, and measuring it precisely is one of the central tasks of a biomechanics laboratory.

The instrument is the **force plate** (or force platform), a rigid plate mounted on **piezoelectric** or **strain-gauge** transducers that resolve the GRF into three orthogonal components:

- The **vertical** component, by far the largest, supports and accelerates the body against gravity. In running it commonly peaks at two to three times **body weight**, and in landing from a jump it can exceed five to ten times body weight.
- The **anteroposterior** (fore-aft) component produces braking on landing and propulsion on push-off.
- The **mediolateral** (side-to-side) component is small in straight running but large in cutting and change-of-direction tasks.

Integrating the GRF over the contact time gives the **impulse**, $J = \int F\,dt$, which by the **impulse-momentum theorem** equals the change in the body's momentum. This is why sprint coaches care not only about how much force is applied but about how it is applied over time: a large net forward impulse is what accelerates the runner.

The force plate also locates the **center of pressure**, the point through which the resultant GRF acts, which is essential for studying balance and gait.

Rotational effects are described by **torque**, also called **moment of force**. Torque is the product of a force and its **moment arm**, the perpendicular distance from the axis of rotation to the line of action of the force:

$$\tau = F \times d$$

A muscle generates joint torque by pulling on a bone at some moment arm from the joint center. Because moment arms are usually short, muscles must generate large forces to produce useful joint torques. The **net joint moment**, computed by a procedure called **inverse dynamics**, combines force-plate data with body-segment kinematics and segment masses to estimate the torque at each joint during movement. Inverse dynamics, formalized for human motion in the twentieth century and built on the **Newton-Euler** equations, is the standard method for estimating the loads that muscles and ligaments experience, information that is impossible to measure directly but vital for understanding both performance and injury risk.

slides.title: Levers, center of mass, gait, and motion capture
slides.body:
The musculoskeletal system is a system of **levers**. A lever is a rigid bar (a bone) that rotates about a fulcrum (a joint) under the influence of an effort (a muscle force) and a load (the resistance). The classification, which dates to **Archimedes**, depends on the arrangement of fulcrum, effort, and load.

- A **first-class lever** has the fulcrum between the effort and the load, like a seesaw. The atlanto-occipital joint of the head on the neck is an example: the neck muscles balance the weight of the head about the joint.
- A **second-class lever** has the load between the fulcrum and the effort, like a wheelbarrow. Rising onto the toes (plantarflexion at the ball of the foot) is the classic human example, and such levers favor force.
- A **third-class lever** has the effort between the fulcrum and the load, like tweezers. **Most human joints are third-class levers**: in elbow flexion the biceps (effort) attaches between the elbow (fulcrum) and the hand holding a weight (load). Third-class levers sacrifice mechanical advantage for **speed and range of motion**, which suits the demands of athletic movement at the cost of requiring large muscle forces.

The **center of mass (COM)**, sometimes called the center of gravity, is the single point at which the body's mass can be considered concentrated for the purposes of analyzing whole-body motion. In an anatomical standing posture it lies roughly anterior to the second sacral vertebra, but it shifts as the limbs move and can even pass outside the body during a high jump, allowing a skilled **Fosbury Flop** jumper to clear a bar that their COM passes beneath. Tracking the COM is essential for studying balance, jumping, and the flight phase of running.

**Gait analysis** applies all of these tools to walking and running. The gait cycle is divided into a **stance phase** and a **swing phase**, further subdivided into events such as initial contact, midstance, and toe-off. Clinical and sport gait labs combine **force plates** with body-segment kinematics to compute joint angles, moments, and powers across the cycle.

The kinematics are captured by **motion capture**. Modern optical systems, such as those made by **Vicon**, use multiple infrared cameras to track reflective markers placed on anatomical landmarks, reconstructing three-dimensional joint positions to sub-millimetre accuracy. Combined with force-plate kinetics and **electromyography** (which records muscle activation), motion capture lets a biomechanist build a complete picture of a movement, from the muscle command to the resulting forces, joint torques, and trajectory of the center of mass.

question.question: Most joints in the human body operate as third-class levers. What is the principal functional consequence of this arrangement?
options: It maximizes mechanical advantage so muscles can be very small.
It favors speed and range of motion at the moving end, at the cost of requiring large muscle forces.
It places the load between the fulcrum and the effort, like a wheelbarrow.
It eliminates the need for the muscle to generate torque.
question.explanation: In a third-class lever the effort (muscle) lies between the fulcrum (joint) and the load, as in elbow flexion by the biceps. This geometry gives a mechanical advantage less than one, so the muscle must produce a force larger than the load, but in exchange the load end moves through a large range and at high speed, which suits athletic movement.

hints: Third-class: effort is between fulcrum and load.
What do you gain if you give up mechanical advantage?
slides.workedSolution: A third-class lever places the muscle's effort between the joint (fulcrum) and the load, as the biceps does in elbow flexion. The effort's moment arm is shorter than the load's, so mechanical advantage is below one and the muscle force must exceed the load. The payoff is that the distal end travels far and fast, favoring speed and range of motion, which is the second option.

question.question: A muscle attaches $3\ \text{cm}$ ($0.03\ \text{m}$) from the elbow joint and pulls with a force of $400\ \text{N}$ perpendicular to the forearm. Using $\tau = F \times d$, compute the torque it generates about the elbow in newton-metres. Give a decimal.
question.hint: Multiply the force by the moment arm in metres.

question.question: Using Newton's second law $F = ma$, what net horizontal force (in newtons) is required to accelerate a $75\ \text{kg}$ sprinter at $4.0\ \text{m/s}^2$? Give the number only.
Use force-plate data to assess a jumper's injury risk.
question.prompt: A volleyball player is referred to your lab after recurrent knee pain. On the force plate, their landings from a spike jump show a very large, sharp vertical ground-reaction-force peak exceeding eight times body weight reached almost instantly, with very little fore-aft braking impulse. Using the impulse-momentum theorem and the idea of net joint moments from inverse dynamics, explain why a rapid, stiff landing concentrates load and increases injury risk, and describe a coaching cue or technique change that would lengthen the contact time and reduce the peak force without changing the athlete's momentum at touchdown.

question.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes kinematics from kinetics?
options: Kinematics studies the forces that cause motion; kinetics describes positions and velocities.
Kinematics describes motion (position, velocity, acceleration) without its causes; kinetics studies the forces and torques that produce motion.
Kinematics and kinetics are synonyms and can be used interchangeably.
Kinematics applies only to rotation, while kinetics applies only to translation.
question.explanation: Kinematics is the geometric description of motion, dealing with displacement, velocity, and acceleration without asking what caused them. Kinetics studies the forces and torques responsible for that motion. Two athletes can show identical kinematics yet experience different kinetics, which is why both analyses are needed.

hints: One half describes motion; the other half explains its causes (forces).
Force plates measure kinetics; video of joint angles measures kinematics.
slides.workedSolution: Kinematics is concerned with the description of motion, such as how fast and in what direction a limb moves, without reference to forces. Kinetics adds the causes, namely the forces and torques producing the motion, measured for example by a force plate and inverse dynamics. The second option captures this distinction precisely.
